summary:
CBRE's 2026 European Office Occupier Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 90 large European office occupiers, finds 65 percent plan to relocate some operations within three years as they chase higher-quality workplaces while resisting premium rents. Nine in ten say they would reject buildings lacking the amenities they need, but willingness to pay extra for those amenities has slipped from 54 percent last year to 48 percent, highlighting tension between quality expectations and cost and space scrutiny.

Space requirements are shifting in type as well as volume. Some 48 percent expect to need more multipurpose and reconfigurable space, 43 percent anticipate demand for specialist facilities such as AI labs, and 38 percent expect to increase use of flexible workspace. Just over half believe AI will eventually reduce both headcount and the amount of space needed, though AI may simultaneously drive demand for more specialised workplace settings as job activities change.

Sustainability continues to shape property decisions, with 45 percent targeting net zero by 2030, up from 37 percent in 2024.

Supply may not keep pace. CBRE forecasts buildings less than five years old will represent just 6.8 percent of European office stock by 2028, the lowest share in over a decade. AI businesses account for roughly 3 percent of European office take-up and favour high-quality central locations, adding to competition.

Anna Esteban, CBRE head of leasing and occupier accounts for Europe, argues firms will occupy less space but be more selective, prioritising workplaces that attract employees and improve experience, which should push more use of flexible workspace to access quality buildings without heavy upfront capital commitment. Mark Cartlich, head of European occupational market research, warns of a mismatch between desired offices and available stock, intensifying competition for prime space. The piece notes findings reflect sentiment among major occupiers rather than the whole market.
